cards.q: What is the difference between a file and a folder?
cards.a: A file is one item (document, photo, program). A folder (directory) is a container that holds files and/or other folders.

cards.q: How do you open File Explorer quickly on Windows?
cards.a: Press Win+E, or click the folder icon on the taskbar, or search 'File Explorer' in the Start menu.

cards.q: In the path C:\Users\You\Documents\report.pdf - what is the path, and what is the filename?
cards.a: The path is the full location (C:\Users\You\Documents\report.pdf). The filename is report.pdf (name + extension).

figure.alt: Path broken into drive, folders, and filename
figure.caption: Path = where; filename = which file

cards.q: Where in File Explorer can you see or type the full path?
cards.a: In the address bar at the top. Click it to reveal/edit the full path (e.g. C:\Users\...).

cards.q: What happens when you delete a file normally, and how do you remove it for good?
cards.a: It usually goes to the Recycle Bin (recoverable). Empty the Recycle Bin, or use Shift+Delete, to remove it permanently (harder to recover).

cards.q: How do you open Windows Settings?
cards.a: Press Win+I, or Start -> Settings (gear icon).

cards.q: What is Task Manager for, and how do you open it?
cards.a: See running apps/processes, CPU/RAM use, and end a frozen program. Open with Ctrl+Shift+Esc (or Ctrl+Alt+Delete -> Task Manager).

figure.alt: Task Manager concept with CPU and memory
figure.caption: Task Manager shows what is running
figure.shows: Task Manager shows what is running

cards.q: Where do browser downloads usually land on Windows?
cards.a: In your Downloads folder (often C:\Users\<you>\Downloads). Check the browser's download list (Ctrl+J in many browsers) for the exact file.

cards.q: What is a file extension (e.g. .pdf, .docx, .exe), and why does it matter?
cards.a: The suffix after the last dot tells Windows (and you) the file type and which app opens it. .exe means a program - don't run unknown ones.

cards.q: How can you make Windows always show file extensions in File Explorer?
cards.a: File Explorer -> View -> Show -> File name extensions (wording can vary slightly by Windows version).

cards.q: Administrator account vs standard user - what's the practical difference?
cards.a: An administrator can install software, change system settings, and manage other accounts. A standard user is limited - safer for everyday use; Windows prompts (UAC) when admin rights are needed.

cards.q: Where do you connect to Wi-Fi or see network status on Windows?
cards.a: Click the network / Wi-Fi icon in the system tray (bottom-right), or Settings -> Network & internet.

cards.q: Where do you check for Windows updates?
cards.a: Settings -> Windows Update. Install updates regularly for security and bug fixes; reboot when asked.

cards.q: How do you safely remove a USB drive?
cards.a: Use 'Eject' / 'Safely remove hardware' on the USB icon in the system tray (or right-click the drive in File Explorer -> Eject) before unplugging, so files finish writing.

cards.q: Cloud storage vs local storage - what's the difference?
cards.a: Local = on this PC (or USB). Cloud = on the internet (OneDrive, Google Drive, etc.) - available on other devices when online; still sync copies may exist locally in a sync folder.

figure.caption: Local on the machine; cloud over the network
figure.shows: Local on the machine; cloud over the network

cards.q: What are the usual shortcuts for copy, cut, and paste?
cards.a: Copy Ctrl+C, Cut Ctrl+X, Paste Ctrl+V. Cut moves; copy duplicates. Works in Explorer and most apps.

cards.q: How do you take a screenshot of part of the screen on modern Windows?
cards.a: Win+Shift+S opens Snipping Tool overlay to select an area. PrtSc copies the whole screen; Win+PrtSc often saves a full-screen shot to Pictures\Screenshots.

cards.q: Desktop vs Documents - how should you think about them?
cards.a: Both are folders under your user profile. Desktop is for quick access (icons on the screen); Documents is a better long-term place for coursework and files you don't need as icons.

cards.q: What's a fast way to find an app or setting without hunting menus?
cards.a: Press the Windows key and start typing the name (e.g. 'Notepad', 'Wi-Fi', 'Task Manager'). Select the result and Enter.

cards.q: What is the difference between the operating system and a web browser?
cards.a: The OS (Windows) runs the whole computer: files, hardware, apps. A browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) is an app for websites - it does not replace the OS.

cards.q: Minimise vs close (X) - what happens to the program?
cards.a: Minimise hides the window but the program keeps running (taskbar). Close (X) exits that window/app (unsaved work may be lost).

cards.q: What does right-click usually do?
cards.a: Opens a context menu with actions for that item (Open, Copy, Rename, Properties, etc.). Very useful in File Explorer and on the desktop.

cards.q: Why open Task Manager when a PC feels slow?
cards.a: Check CPU, memory, and disk usage to see which process is consuming resources (Ctrl+Shift+Esc).

cards.q: Why can file extensions matter for security?
cards.a: The extension hints at the file type (e.g. .exe vs .pdf). Malware may disguise dangerous types; show extensions in Explorer to avoid surprises.

cards.q: When should you use an administrator account?
cards.a: Only when needed to install software or change system settings - daily browsing/email as a standard user reduces impact of mistakes and malware.

cards.q: What is a risk of assuming
cards.a: Sync conflicts, accidental deletes, or account lockout can lose access - keep important local copies and know where the authoritative file lives.

cards.q: Why install OS and app updates promptly?
cards.a: Updates often patch security vulnerabilities and fix bugs - delaying leaves known holes open.

cards.q: What is a basic caution on public Wi-Fi?
cards.a: Avoid sensitive logins on untrusted networks when possible; prefer HTTPS and consider a trusted network/VPN policy for confidential work.
